about: The film's voice. Times are in seconds of the film, as data-at in index.html: every source time in film.html after 34.6 s is 2.4 s later in the film. A line without 'at' follows the one before it after 'pause' seconds. 'say' is how a line is spoken, where that differs from how it is written; 'text' is what the captions show.

lines.text: The phone page sends files between an iPhone and a Windows PC, over plain Wi-Fi.
AirDrop needs Apple's own radio link, AWDL, and Windows can't run it.
lines.say: AirDrop needs Apple's own radio link, A-W-D-L, and Windows can't run it.

lines.text: So the phone page uses the Wi-Fi both devices already share.
The PC shows a QR code, and the iPhone's camera reads it.
It holds the PC's address and a secret token, new every run.
Safari opens the page.
Pick five photos and tap Send.
The upload is one request, and its order is the point: first the device, then the list of files, then the files.
The PC reads the list, then stops and asks, before it reads a single byte of the files.
The phone has to wait.
Accept, and the photos stream across at Wi-Fi speed.
They're saved together, or not at all.
What you agree to is what gets saved.
Files keep their listed names. If one is bigger than listed, or the count is off, nothing is kept.
This time, one photo.
Decline it, and the phone is told at once.
Nothing is left behind on the PC.
Files can go the other way too.
While the sheet is open, the PC offers files, and the phone saves them to its Files app.
Links to an old offer stop working.
Two locks keep it safe: the secret token in the address, and the question on the PC.
It's plain HTTP, so use it on a network you trust.
These four were tested with a real iPhone, on iOS 27.
Not AirDrop. Just the Wi-Fi you already have.
